dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference

evidence.note: Read both fixture next-shims.d.ts files and multiple fixture layouts/pages/middleware early — genuine contract inference from the fixtures' declared type shims.

Only ran `ls` on /opt/reference/node_modules and next/dist; never opened the vendored vite/next .d.ts types, next-source, or vite-source. Considered adapting reference code but abandoned it and proceeded from Next.js memory.
Consulted e2e spec files (grep/cat) to derive expected behavior for specific subsystems — grounding some contracts in the test suite rather than pure memory.

When Vite plugin alias/ssrLoadModule resolution was ambiguous, the agent reasoned/guessed about Vite internals ('maybe Vite caches optimizeDeps', 'alias not invoked') instead of re-consulting the vendored vite source.
RSC/caching semantics repeatedly labeled a 'rabbit hole' and skipped rather than researched in the vendored plugin-rsc/next source.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent solidly mined the fixture side — reading both next-shims.d.ts files and ~38 fixture files plus e2e specs, grounding the next/* contracts (satisfying half of anchor 5). But the Vite plugin API surface and the vendored Vite/Next.js source were never actually read (only `ls`'d), and the Vite lifecycle was worked from memory with ambiguity resolved by guessing rather than source consultation; RSC/cache semantics were skipped as a rabbit hole. This places it above anchor 3 (more than a cursory shim skim) but clearly below anchor 5 (which requires reading the relevant Vite plugin API surface), landing at 4.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: First real decomposition: a numbered list of subsystems (package/bin, CLI dev/build/start, Vite plugin, pages router SSR, app router, middleware...). It mirrors the requirement bullets and has an implied 'foundation-first' order but no explicit done-criteria per milestone — flat-list flavored (anchor 3-5 territory).

Reached a minimal end-to-end path early — dev server + basic pages rendering, then ran the suite for a 34/325 baseline before layering features. This 'thin vertical slice first, then layer' behavior and tying next work to concrete test buckets ('big targets: app router route handlers, pages') pushes above 5.

Sequencing was dependency-aware in spots (resolution/plugin/CLI before routing before SSR; got client navigation working to 'unlock ~20 tests') and each target explicitly tied to fixtures/test counts, an 8-flavored trait.

But subsystem interfaces were not explicitly managed: adding middleware regressed 73→25 because it consumed the request body — coupling surprised the agent rather than being planned for, forcing reactive backtracking rather than milestone re-planning.

Late trajectory shows greedy, test-count-driven target selection ('big bucket left is app router CSR') and repeated revert/re-add cycles (hydration reverts). Progress tracked as a running pass count (215→221) but never against an explicit milestone plan with done-criteria; decomposition stayed emergent, not a living milestone structure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent identified the major subsystems and picked a sensible dependency order (plugin/CLI → pages routing → SSR → app router → middleware/cache), and notably established a minimal end-to-end slice early and used the Playwright suite to gate each subsequent step — traits of the 8 anchor. However, the decomposition itself was a flat requirement-mirroring list without explicit per-milestone done-criteria, and sequencing after the baseline was greedy-by-test-bucket rather than a maintained dependency-aware milestone plan; interface coupling between subsystems was discovered through regressions (middleware body, hydration/templates) rather than deliberately managed. This lands solidly between the 5 and 8 anchors, closer to 5, i.e. a 6.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Stood up vinext dev servers manually on dedicated ports and hit endpoints with curl to observe SSR/API/route-handler behavior between slow full-suite runs — targeted manual fixture verification.
Wrote a standalone Playwright script (/tmp/test-nav.cjs) as a minimal browser reproduction to isolate a client hydration/navigation bug, then verified the fix before re-running the suite.
Diagnosed a 73->25 regression by root cause (stale node_modules dist, script-src mismatch) using curl probes and dist inspection rather than blindly re-running or symptom-patching.
Parsed playwright-env-results.json and grepped results by subsystem to cluster failures and pick next targets, using the suite as a per-subsystem diagnostic.
Repeatedly read specific .spec.ts files to learn exact expected behavior before implementing/fixing a subsystem.
Ran full suite as final regression gate; build verified, but production 'vinext start' path never independently exercised (all manual probes used dev).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it runs subsystem-focused checks (curl probes against manually-started dev servers, results.json parsing, spec reading) and uses failures to drive fixes, verifying dev and build. It reaches toward level 8 by designing a real verification loop that stands up fixtures manually to observe SSR/API/middleware behavior, treats the full suite as a regression gate, and even builds one browser-based minimal reproduction with root-cause regression diagnosis. It falls short of a full 8/10 because the fast layer is entirely curl-based (no targeted Playwright subsets), the production start path is never independently confirmed, and the minimal-repro/probing effort is a one-off rather than a systematic layered strategy across the hard subsystems — placing it at 7.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Parsed results JSON to track '73/325 from 34' and categorized remaining failures by subsystem (app-router route handlers, pages-router client nav) to pick targets — structured pass-rate-by-area view.
Detected sharp regression 73→25 after adding middleware/pages-client, investigated which subsystems regressed, and traced/fixed the cause rather than blindly retrying.
Recorded '191/325! Big jump from 164 (+27)' and enumerated remaining test categories, quantifying progress toward the full suite and reallocating effort.

Recognized it was looping on app-router hydration that repeatedly regressed pass counts (212, then 220→180); stepped back and reverted, then diagnosed a subtle cross-subsystem bug where the app bootstrap edit overwrote the pages-router client bootstrap.
Reconciled 'Back to 220/325... same as before the regression' and confirmed stable final count 221/325, maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture (remaining = RSC/CSR hydration) to the end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a structured, continually-updated view of pass-rate by subsystem, re-ran the full suite after nearly every change, quantified progress with deltas toward the full suite, and repeatedly detected regressions caused by touching shared bootstrap/hydration code — reverting and diagnosing rather than looping blindly (steps 436, 501-530). This squarely matches the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because regressions were caught reactively after full runs rather than early, and its count model was occasionally imprecise/confused (steps 134, 204, 513).

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence

evidence.note: Recognized the monkey-patch/__navigate client-navigation scheme was fundamentally broken (read-only imports) and reworked it into a proper settable setNavigator design — a real subsystem rework, not a patch.

Diagnosed alias resolution issues and switched the render pipeline from renderToString to renderToPipeableStream/renderToReadableStream to support async pages, unlocking +27 tests (164→191); a foundational render-pipeline revision.

Reworked the params model into a Promise that is also sync-accessible (Object.assign(Promise.resolve(params), params)) after discovering fixtures mix sync and async access — adapting design to falsified assumptions.

Repeatedly attempted app-router hydration, saw regressions (220→180), and reverted each time; ultimately avoided/deferred the RSC-hydration foundation as 'too complex' and leaned on native browser behavior — workaround preference with churn rather than a clean foundational pivot.

After a 73→25 regression from adding middleware, traced it to response-ordering (applyMw after res.end) and fixed the ordering; effective local correction but of a specific bug, not a design-level revision.
Recovered a large self-inflicted regression (an over-broad sed clobbered the pages client bootstrap) by restoring the entry — defensive repair, re-verified by re-running the suite back to 220.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly moves above anchor 3: it revisits and reworks underlying subsystem designs (client navigation from monkey-patch to setNavigator, render pipeline from renderToString to streaming, params to a dual Promise/sync model) and absorbs the cost rather than only patching — matching anchor 5. However, on the single biggest foundational blocker (real RSC/hydration) it declined to refactor the foundation, instead cycling through hydration attempts and reverts and deferring to workarounds, and its largest corrections were bug/regression recoveries rather than deliberate foundational pivots with re-verified dependents. That keeps it at 5, short of anchor 8's deliberate foundational refactor.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite

evidence.note: Implemented middleware config.matcher as a general mechanism rather than special-casing the '/api' skip the one failing test wanted — reads config and honors matcher, a real Next.js contract.
Added generateStaticParams/dynamicParams 404 logic, revalidate-based Cache-Control, and ISR caching keyed by pathname — general semantics, not per-fixture hardcodes.

Chose sync params over Next 16's Promise params specifically because the visible fixture accesses params.id synchronously; fit to the fixture's style with no note about the hidden-suite risk of diverging from the real contract.
Tuned metadata keywords join to the exact string ('test,metadata,vinext') the visible test asserts — matching an exact expected output rather than reasoning about general formatting.

Throughout, work is driven by 'grep the spec to see what the test wants' then fix; final summary lists subsystems but never once reasons about the 373 hidden tests or generalizing beyond the visible sample.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent overwhelmingly implemented real framework mechanisms (filesystem routing, config matchers, generateStaticParams, ISR keyed by path, metadata generation, 405 handling) rather than hardcoding fixture outputs, placing it well above the 0-3 hack anchors. But it never explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, never stress-tests beyond the visible fixtures, and occasionally fits to exact test expectations (keywords string format, sync params to match the fixture) without noting overfit risk. This matches the level-5 anchor — actual semantics per behavior, aware the suite is a sample only implicitly — and falls short of the level-8 anchor's explicit gap reasoning and deliberate generalization to the upstream contract.

rubric.task_read: This is a maximally long-horizon, high-complexity build: reimplement the core of Next.js (CLI, Pages + App routers, SSR, SSG, `use cache`, server actions, middleware, `after()`, client hooks, and a Vite plugin that shims `next/*`) as a single `vinext` package on Vite's plugin API, with no internet and only vendored source to learn from. Difficulty comes from the sheer surface area, tightly-coupled subsystems, contracts that must be reverse-engineered from vendored Next.js/Vite source and fixture `next-shims.d.ts`, and a moving target (335 visible → 373 hidden tests). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty; ceremony risk is low, thrash-and-lose-the-plot risk is very high.

dimensions.name: Reference mining & contract inference
dimensions.description: Studying vendored Vite/Next.js source and fixture type shims to understand the Vite plugin API and the exact `next/*` contracts before and while implementing, rather than guessing framework semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There is no internet; correct behavior lives entirely in the vendored source and the fixtures' `next-shims.d.ts`. Guessing Next.js semantics or the Vite plugin lifecycle guarantees rework across a huge surface.

anchors.0: Starts coding shims/routing from memory of Next.js without opening any reference or fixture file.
anchors.3: Skims one or two reference files or a fixture shim, then proceeds mostly on assumption; contracts are inferred loosely.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant Vite plugin API surface and the fixture `next-shims.d.ts` for the subsystem currently being built; grounds each `next/*` shim in an actual type signature.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the vendored Next.js source and Vite plugin hooks to the required subsystems, extracts precise contracts from every fixture shim, and re-consults source when behavior is ambiguous rather than guessing; notes non-obvious semantics (e.g. RSC boundaries, cache keys, action serialization).
anchors.10: Sustained, targeted research throughout the build: continuously cross-references upstream source to resolve edge-case semantics as they surface, distinguishes what the fixtures actually require from full Next.js behavior, and builds an accurate mental/written model of how routing, RSC, and module resolution interlock — visibly preventing whole classes of rework.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the framework into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (module shim/resolution, dev server, routing, SSR, SSG, caching, actions, CLI/build) with a dependency-aware sequence and done-criteria per milestone.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The subsystems are tightly coupled and one package must ship all of them; without dependency-aware sequencing and explicit milestones the agent will build in an order that forces constant backtracking and never reaches a testable state.

anchors.0: Treats the whole thing as one undifferentiated coding push; no ordering or sub-goals.
anchors.3: A flat, generic list mirroring the requirement bullets, with no dependency ordering or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Identifies the major subsystems and picks a sensible order (e.g. resolution/plugin before routing before SSR/SSG), with a rough notion of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences a minimal end-to-end path (one route rendering under dev) before layering features, each milestone tied to concrete fixtures/tests that prove it, and revisited as the build reveals coupling.
anchors.10: A living decomposition that establishes a thin vertical slice early, orders remaining subsystems to maximize how soon tests can gate progress, explicitly manages interfaces between subsystems so they compose, and re-plans milestone boundaries as integration realities emerge — never losing the through-line across the long horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately using and extending the Playwright suite and fixture apps as checks — running targeted subsets per subsystem, building smaller probes, and verifying behavior beyond just 'it compiles'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 335-test suite is the ground truth, but it is slow and coarse; verifying each subsystem needs faster, targeted checks and running the right fixtures, or the agent flies blind between rare full-suite runs.

anchors.0: Never runs the test suite or the fixture apps; assumes correctness from the code alone.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as a pass/fail oracle with no targeted or intermediate verification.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets / individual fixtures for the subsystem in progress and uses failures to guide fixes; verifies dev and build paths work.
anchors.8: Designs a verification loop: fast targeted checks per subsystem, standing up fixtures manually to observe SSR/SSG/action behavior, and using the suite as a regression gate rather than a debugger; confirms both `dev` and the production `build`/`start` paths.
anchors.10: Builds a deliberate, layered verification strategy — minimal reproductions for hard subsystems (RSC, caching, actions), interprets test failures by root cause rather than symptom, and actively probes behaviors the visible suite may under-cover, treating passing tests as necessary-not-sufficient evidence of a faithful reimplementation.

dimensions.name: Progress & pass-rate tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems/tests pass vs. remain, and detecting circular debugging or regressions across a very large surface.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of tests and many interdependent subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to fix one area while regressing another, or to loop on the same failure; an accurate done-vs-remaining picture is what sustains forward motion.

anchors.0: No tracking of what passes or what is left; works reactively with no sense of overall state.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; notices only whatever failure is in front of it.
anchors.5: Tracks pass counts / which subsystems are done and which are pending, and re-checks after changes to catch obvious regressions.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, updated view of pass-rate by area, watches for regressions when touching shared code, and recognizes when it is looping on one failure and steps back rather than retrying blindly.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise model of done-vs-remaining against real test evidence across the whole surface, catches subtle cross-subsystem regressions early, quantifies progress toward the full suite, and reallocates effort to the highest-leverage remaining failures rather than drifting.

dimensions.name: Design revision under divergence
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach (module resolution scheme, rendering pipeline, cache/action wiring) when reality — failing tests or discovered semantics — contradicts the initial design, rather than patching around a flawed foundation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early architectural choices (how `next/*` is intercepted, how RSC/SSR is wired into Vite) will be partly wrong; the agent must be willing to refactor the foundation instead of piling hacks that make later subsystems impossible.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on the original approach even as failures accumulate; only adds patches.
anchors.3: Makes local fixes when something breaks but never revisits an underlying design decision even when it is clearly the cause.
anchors.5: Recognizes when an approach is wrong and reworks that subsystem, absorbing the cost rather than hacking around it.
anchors.8: Detects when a foundational choice (resolution, render pipeline) is blocking multiple subsystems and refactors it deliberately, updating the plan and re-verifying dependents afterward.
anchors.10: Treats falsified assumptions as signals to rethink the design cleanly, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes foundational pivots without losing already-passing behavior, and emerges with a more coherent architecture — demonstrating sustained self-correction across the horizon.

dimensions.name: Resisting overfit to the visible suite
dimensions.description: Implementing faithful, general framework behavior rather than special-casing the 335 visible tests, given explicit notice that 373 hidden tests over the same behavior will judge the work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The spec openly states the final grade uses a larger hidden suite covering the same behaviors; an agent that hard-codes to visible fixtures will pass locally and fail the real metric, so recognizing and countering this gap is a distinct, decisive meta-work demand.

anchors.0: Hard-codes outputs or narrowly special-cases the visible fixtures/tests to turn them green.
anchors.3: Mostly general but reaches for a fixture-specific shortcut when a behavior is hard, without noting the risk.
anchors.5: Implements the actual semantics for each behavior rather than test-specific hacks, aware the suite is a sample not the target.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the visible-vs-hidden gap, generalizes each subsystem to the real Next.js contract from the reference, and avoids overfitting even under schedule pressure.
anchors.10: Systematically implements to the general contract inferred from upstream source and shim types, stress-tests behaviors beyond what the visible tests exercise to expose overfit, and can articulate why the implementation should hold on unseen cases of the same behavior.
